section.title: The Ten Commandments Restated
section.sectionRationale: As the covenant renewal proper begins, Moses restates the Ten Commandments given at Horeb to the generation now poised to enter the land, grounding the whole book's statutes and ordinances in these same ten words spoken by God Himself.
section.thesis: Standing at the border of the land, Moses restates the Ten Commandments given at Horeb to the new generation, reminding them that the LORD spoke these words directly, face to face, and that Israel's own trembling request for a mediator reveals both God's holiness and their need for someone to stand between them and Him.
section.frameNote: Seven movements: the covenant made at Horeb, with this generation; no other gods and no idols; the name of the LORD; the Sabbath, grounded in deliverance from slavery; honoring father and mother; the five commands concerning neighbor; and the people's fear and their request for a mediator.

units.label: The covenant made at Horeb, with us

verses.text: Then Moses summoned all Israel and said to them: Hear, O Israel, the statutes and ordinances that I declare in your hearing this day. Learn them and observe them carefully.
The LORD our God made a covenant with us at Horeb.
He did not make this covenant with our fathers, but with all of us who are alive here today.
The LORD spoke with you {{panim|face to face}} out of the fire on the mountain.
At that time I was standing between the LORD and you to declare to you the word of the LORD, because you were afraid of the fire and would not go up the mountain. And He said:
“I am the LORD your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt, out of the house of slavery.
You shall have no other gods before Me.
You shall not make for yourself an idol in the form of anything in the heavens above, on the earth below, or in the waters beneath.

You shall not bow down to them or worship them; for I, the LORD your God, am a jealous God, visiting the iniquity of the fathers on their children to the third and fourth generations of those who hate Me,
but showing loving devotion to a thousand generations of those who love Me and keep My commandments.
You shall not take the name of the LORD your God in vain, for the LORD will not leave anyone unpunished who takes His name in vain.

units.label: The Sabbath, grounded in deliverance
units.note: remember that you were a slave

verses.text: Observe the Sabbath day by keeping it holy, as the LORD your God has commanded you.
Six days you shall labor and do all your work,

but the seventh day is a Sabbath to the LORD your God, on which you must not do any work, neither you, nor your son or daughter, nor your manservant or maidservant, nor your ox or donkey or any of your livestock, nor the foreigner within your gates, so that your manservant and maidservant may rest as you do.

Remember that you were a slave in the land of Egypt, and that the LORD your God brought you out of there with a mighty hand and an outstretched arm. That is why the LORD your God has commanded you to keep the Sabbath day.

units.label: Honor father and mother
units.note: so that it may go well with you

verses.text: Honor your father and your mother, as the LORD your God has commanded you, so that your days may be long and that it may go well with you in the land that the LORD your God is giving you.
You shall not murder.
You shall not commit adultery.
You shall not steal.
You shall not bear false witness against your neighbor.

You shall not {{chamad|covet}} your neighbor's wife. You shall not covet your neighbor's house or field, or his manservant or maidservant, or his ox or donkey, or anything that belongs to your neighbor.”

units.label: The people's fear, and a mediator

verses.text: The LORD spoke these commandments in a loud voice to your whole assembly out of the fire, the cloud, and the deep darkness on the mountain; He added nothing more. And He wrote them on two tablets of stone and gave them to me.
And when you heard the voice out of the darkness while the mountain was blazing with fire, all the heads of your tribes and your elders approached me,
and you said, “Behold, the LORD our God has shown us His glory and greatness, and we have heard His voice out of the fire. Today we have seen that a man can live even if God speaks with him.
But now, why should we die? For this great fire will consume us, and we will die, if we hear the voice of the LORD our God any longer.
For who of all flesh has heard the voice of the living God speaking out of the fire, as we have, and survived?
Go near and listen to all that the LORD our God says. Then you can tell us everything the LORD our God tells you; we will listen and obey.”
And the LORD heard the words you spoke to me, and He said to me, “I have heard the words that these people have spoken to you. They have done well in all that they have spoken.
If only they had such a heart to fear Me and keep all My commandments always, so that it might be well with them and with their children forever.
Go and tell them: ‘Return to your tents.’
But you stand here with Me, that I may speak to you all the commandments and statutes and ordinances you are to teach them to follow in the land that I am giving them to possess.”
So be careful to do as the LORD your God has commanded you; you are not to turn aside to the right or to the left.
You must walk in all the ways that the LORD your God has commanded you, so that you may live and prosper and prolong your days in the land that you will possess.

panim.gloss: Face to face. Describes the directness and intimacy of the LORD's speech at Horeb, not that Israel literally saw God's form, but that His words came without any human intermediary, making Israel's request for a mediator in this same chapter all the more striking.

chamad.gloss: To covet, to desire strongly, often with a view to taking. Unlike the other nine commands, which address outward acts, this one names the internal desire itself as sin, addressing the heart's longing before it ever becomes an action.

basic.context: Moses restates the Ten Commandments to the generation about to enter the land, reminding them that these words were spoken directly by God at Horeb to their own generation, not merely to their parents, and that this same generation once begged for a mediator because God's direct voice terrified them.
basic.hermeneutics: This is a real, historical covenant renewal, restating unchanging commands for a new audience. Christians today are not bound to Israel's specific national covenant form, but the moral substance, love for God and neighbor, remains the abiding, unchanging expression of God's character.
basic.originalLanguages: The LORD spoke panim el panim, face to face, meaning directly and without a human intermediary, which makes Israel's fear and their request for Moses to mediate all the more significant. The tenth command addresses chamad, covetous desire itself, naming an inward longing as sin before it ever becomes an outward act.
basic.typology: Israel's terror before God's direct voice and their request for Moses to stand between them and God anticipates the greater mediation of Christ, who alone can bring sinners into God's presence without terror, Hebrews 12:18-24.
basic.christ: Hebrews 12:18-24 draws directly on this scene, contrasting the terrifying, untouchable mountain of Sinai with the access believers now have to God through Jesus, the mediator of a new covenant, whose blood speaks a better word than the fear this chapter records.
basic.god: God is holy enough that His own redeemed people cannot bear the sound of His unmediated voice, yet He is also relational enough to commend their fear as 'doing well' and to long for a heart in them that would keep His commandments forever out of love, not merely terror.
basic.crossReferences: Exodus 20:1-21 records the first giving of these same commandments at Horeb. Hebrews 12:18-24 contrasts the terror of Sinai with the access believers now have through Christ. Matthew 22:37-40 summarizes the whole law as love for God and neighbor.
basic.oneStory: God gives His unchanging moral law directly to His redeemed people, and their instinctive fear before His unmediated voice reveals humanity's deep need for a mediator. That need is finally met in Jesus Christ, the one mediator who brings God's people near without terror and writes this same law on their hearts.

context.literary:
Deuteronomy 5 opens Moses' second and longest address. The BSB footnote at 5:1 observes that everything from here to 26:19 can be read as one unbroken speech, and this chapter is its foundation stone. What follows in chapters 6 to 11 presses the heart of the ten words, especially the first, and chapters 12 to 26 then work out the statutes and ordinances that verse 31 says Moses received while the people waited in their tents. Many readers have noticed that those later laws follow the order of the commandments in a loose way, worship first, then the name, then sacred time, then authority, life, marriage, property and truthful speech.

The chapter itself is built as a frame around a centre. Verses 1 to 5 and 22 to 33 are narrative and exhortation; verses 6 to 21 are the words God spoke. The frame opens with 'Hear, O Israel ... observe them carefully,' verse 1, and closes with 'be careful to do,' verse 32, the same verb for keeping or guarding at both ends. The promise of long days in the land sounds at verse 16 and again at verse 33, tying the whole to life in Canaan.

Inside the ten words the Sabbath command is the longest, and Deuteronomy shapes it into a hinge. Its list of those who must rest, 'your manservant and maidservant ... your ox or donkey,' verse 14, reappears almost exactly in the tenth command, verse 21. The day that belongs to God is also the day that protects the neighbour, so the command about sacred time reaches forward into the commands about the neighbour's household.

Verse 22 then draws a firm line: 'He added nothing more.' The ten words stand apart as the only speech Israel heard directly. Everything after verse 31 comes through Moses, which is why the rest of the book is Moses speaking.
context.historical:
Moses speaks on the plains of Moab, east of the Jordan, in the fortieth year after the exodus, Deuteronomy 1:3 and 1:5. Nearly everyone who had been an adult at Horeb was dead. Numbers 14:29 had sentenced all those twenty years and older to fall in the wilderness, and Deuteronomy 2:14 records that the whole generation of fighting men had perished. Many of those listening had stood at the mountain as children, and many more had been born on the journey since. That is the pressure behind verse 3, with its piled up pronouns: with us, we, these, here, today, all of us, living.

The covenant form would have been familiar in outline. Treaties between a great king and a lesser people in the second millennium BC often began by naming the king, recalled what he had done for his vassal, and then laid down the obligations that loyalty required. The ten words move in the same way. 'I am the LORD your God,' verse 6, names the King; 'who brought you out of the land of Egypt,' recalls His deed; the commands follow as the shape of a grateful allegiance. Some suggest the two tablets were duplicate copies, one for each party, as treaty documents were kept, and later both were laid in the ark, Deuteronomy 10:1-5 and 1 Kings 8:9.

The Sabbath grounding in slavery spoke to real life. Israel would soon own servants, fields and working animals. Deuteronomy returns again and again to the refrain 'Remember that you were slaves in Egypt,' Deuteronomy 15:15, 16:12 and 24:18, each time to soften the treatment of the weak. Israel's neighbours had law collections, such as the code of Hammurabi, but a weekly rest that reached slaves, foreigners and beasts of burden is one of the distinctive marks of Israel's law. A people who had worked without rest under Pharaoh were not to become Pharaoh to others.
context.canonical:
Scripture records the ten words twice, at Exodus 20:1-17 and here, and it calls them the words of the covenant, Exodus 34:28 and Deuteronomy 4:13. The tablets were written by the finger of God, Exodus 31:18 and Deuteronomy 9:10, broken after the golden calf, rewritten, and placed in the ark, where 1 Kings 8:9 still finds them in Solomon's temple. The prophets indict Israel by the same list. Hosea 4:2 names cursing, lying, murder, stealing and adultery; Jeremiah 7:9 asks, 'Will you steal and murder, commit adultery and perjury, burn incense to Baal, and follow other gods?' Psalm 81:9-10 echoes the prologue and the first command in one breath.

The second half of the chapter has its own long future. Deuteronomy 18:16-18 recalls the people's plea at Horeb, 'Let us not hear the voice of the LORD our God,' and God's answer that they had spoken well, and from that moment comes the promise of a prophet like Moses. Peter and Stephen both apply that promise to Jesus, Acts 3:22 and 7:37. God's wish in verse 29 for a people with 'such a heart' opens a line that runs through Deuteronomy 30:6, where He promises to circumcise their hearts, to Jeremiah 31:33 and Ezekiel 36:26-27.

The New Testament cites the commandments often, as the BSB footnotes show. Jesus lists them to the rich young man, Matthew 19:18-19 and Mark 10:19, and deepens murder and adultery to anger and lust, Matthew 5:21-28. Paul says he would not have known coveting without the tenth word, Romans 7:7, and sums up the second table in love, Romans 13:9. Ephesians 6:2-3 calls honouring parents the first commandment with a promise. Hebrews 12:18-24 sets the burning mountain of this chapter beside Mount Zion.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Moses wanted a generation that had not been adults at Horeb to hear the ten words as addressed to them, not as a family heirloom. That is why he tells the story of the mountain in the second person, 'The LORD spoke with you,' verse 4, even though many of his hearers were children at the time or not yet born. Every generation of Israel was to stand at Horeb by hearing this word.

He also wanted them to see the order of grace and command. The first words are not a demand but a self-introduction and a reminder of rescue, verse 6. Obedience is the response of the freed, not the price of freedom.

By retelling the people's fear in verses 23 to 27, Moses explains his own role and the authority of everything he is about to say. The people asked for a mediator and God approved it, verse 28. The statutes of chapters 12 to 26 therefore carry God's authority though they come through Moses' mouth. Finally, God's own sigh in verse 29 shows Moses' deepest concern: that Israel would have a heart to match their promise, 'we will listen and obey,' verse 27. The rest of Deuteronomy keeps returning to that heart.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The chapter mixes narrative and command, and the two need to be kept distinct. The scene at Horeb, the fire, the cloud and the people's retreat to their tents, is recorded history. It is not a pattern for how believers now meet God; Hebrews 12:18-24 insists that Christians have come to a different mountain.

The ten words themselves are commands, addressed to Israel as a redeemed nation about to live in a particular land, with promises tied to that land, verses 16 and 33. The moral substance of the commands is restated throughout the New Testament: worship of the one God, rejection of idols, reverence for His name, honour for parents, and the protection of life, marriage, property, truth and the heart's desires, Romans 13:9 and Ephesians 6:2-3. The Sabbath is the one command whose form the New Testament treats differently, calling it a shadow whose substance belongs to Christ, Colossians 2:16-17, while the rest it provides remains for God's people, Hebrews 4:9. Believers still hear the principle of verse 14, that rest and mercy should reach the weakest in the household.

debates.question: Why does Deuteronomy ground the Sabbath command in deliverance from Egypt (v.15) while Exodus 20:11 grounds it in God's rest after creation?

views.label: Complementary reasons for one command
views.case: Both motives are true and belong together. Exodus 20:11 roots the rhythm of work and rest in God's own week of creation; Deuteronomy adds the memory of slavery. Nothing in either text denies the other, and Deuteronomy's own 'as the LORD your God has commanded you,' verse 12, points back to an earlier giving of the command.

views.label: The emphasis shifts to suit the audience and purpose
views.case: Deuteronomy is preached to a people about to own land, servants and livestock. Moses therefore foregrounds the purpose clause, 'so that your manservant and maidservant may rest as you do,' verse 14, and the memory of their own bondage. The change from 'Remember' in Exodus 20:8 to 'Observe' here fits a sermon that stresses keeping and doing.

views.label: Creation and redemption as one pattern
views.case: Some note that redemption in Scripture is repeatedly pictured as new creation. The God who rested from making the world also brought Israel out of Egypt into rest, so the two reasons are two panels of one theology, which Hebrews 4:9-10 later gathers into the rest that remains for God's people.

debates.bearing: The Sabbath reflects God as both Creator and Redeemer, and Deuteronomy's pastoral weight falls on mercy: the rest God gives His freed people must be shared with the powerless. Jesus' Sabbath healings, such as the woman 'released from her bondage on the Sabbath day,' Luke 13:16, show the redemption motive at full strength.

debates.question: How should the ten words be numbered?

views.label: Jewish tradition
views.case: The first word is the self-introduction of verse 6, 'I am the LORD your God,' and the second joins the ban on other gods with the ban on images, verses 7 to 10. Coveting, verse 21, is one command.

views.label: Augustine, Roman Catholic and Lutheran tradition
views.case: Verses 6 to 10 are one command about exclusive worship, with images treated as an expression of other gods. The tenth word is split in two. Deuteronomy gives some support to this, because it places the neighbour's wife first and uses a separate verb for her, then a second verb for house, field and goods, verse 21.

views.label: Reformed, Orthodox and most early Christian tradition
views.case: Other gods, verse 7, and idols, verses 8 to 10, are two distinct commands, one concerning the object of worship and the other its manner, and coveting is a single command. This reading follows the pattern known from early Jewish writers such as Philo and Josephus.

debates.bearing: Scripture says there are ten words, Deuteronomy 4:13, but never numbers them. The numbering matters mainly for whether the ban on images is heard as its own command. On any count, verse 8 forbids making an image of God, not only worshipping other gods, and Deuteronomy 4:15 grounds it in the fact that Israel saw no form at Horeb.

debates.question: What does verse 3 mean when it says the covenant was not made 'with our fathers'?

views.label: The patriarchs
views.case: 'Fathers' in Deuteronomy often means Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, Deuteronomy 6:10 and 9:5. On this reading Moses is saying that the covenant at Horeb was something new, not made with the patriarchs, but with the nation redeemed from Egypt.

views.label: An emphatic 'not only'
views.case: Others read the verse as rhetorical emphasis: the covenant was not merely for the previous generation, now dead, but for those alive today. Hebrew sometimes states a contrast absolutely to mean 'not so much this as that,' and Deuteronomy 29:14-15 extends the covenant even to 'those who are not here today.'

debates.bearing: Either way the verse makes the covenant present tense. The hearers cannot treat Horeb as their parents' experience. Deuteronomy's constant 'today' invites every later reader into the same position.

study.originalLanguages:
Scripture never calls these 'the ten commandments' in the Hebrew. The phrase in Deuteronomy 4:13, 10:4 and Exodus 34:28 is literally 'the ten words,' aseret ha-devarim, which the BSB renders 'the Ten Commandments.' The Greek form of that phrase gives the English word Decalogue. The designation fits verse 22: these are words God spoke aloud, and He 'added nothing more.'

In verse 4 the phrase is panim be-panim, 'face in face,' a slightly different wording from panim el panim, 'face to face,' used of Moses in Exodus 33:11 and Deuteronomy 34:10. Deuteronomy is careful here. Israel heard God directly, yet 'saw no form,' Deuteronomy 4:12 and 4:15. The directness is in the voice, not in any sight of God.

The Sabbath command opens with a different verb from Exodus. Exodus 20:8 says zakhor, 'Remember'; Deuteronomy 5:12 says shamor, 'Observe' or 'keep.' The verb shamar is the one that frames the chapter, 'observe them carefully,' verse 1, and 'be careful,' verse 32. Remembering is still present, but it moves to verse 15: 'Remember that you were a slave.' Deuteronomy also adds 'as the LORD your God has commanded you' to both the Sabbath and the parents' command, verses 12 and 16, pointing back to the first giving.

The third command forbids taking the name 'in vain,' la-shav. The verb is nasa, to lift or carry, as one lifts a name in an oath or bears it as one's own. Shav means emptiness or worthlessness. Exodus 20:16 forbids 'false witness' with the word sheqer, a lie. Deuteronomy 5:20 uses shav instead, an 'empty' witness. The same word now stands behind the third and the ninth commands, so that emptying God's name and emptying one's testimony against a neighbour are linked.

The tenth command uses two verbs. For the neighbour's wife it keeps chamad, the verb of Exodus 20:17. For house, field and goods it uses a different verb, titavveh, from avah, to crave or long for, the verb behind the 'strong craving' of the rabble in Numbers 11:4. Both roots meet in Genesis 3:6, where the tree is 'pleasing to the eyes,' a form of avah, and 'desirable,' a form of chamad. Deuteronomy also moves the wife ahead of the house and adds 'field,' a detail that suits a people about to receive land.

In Hebrew the commands of verses 18 to 21 are joined by 'and': 'and you shall not commit adultery, and you shall not steal.' Exodus lists them without the conjunction. Deuteronomy binds the neighbour commands into one chain, the point James makes in James 2:10-11.

Two expressions in God's speech deserve notice. 'Jealous God' in verse 9 is el qanna, the burning zeal of a husband who will not share his bride; Exodus 34:14 says His very name is Jealous. And verse 29 begins with mi yitten, literally 'who will give,' the normal Hebrew idiom for an intense wish. God Himself voices the longing that someone would give Israel such a heart, a longing He answers in Deuteronomy 30:6.

typology.type: Moses standing between the LORD and the people (v.5)
typology.fulfillment: Moses stood between a holy God and a frightened people, heard His words, and carried them down. Deuteronomy 18:15-18 builds a promise on this very scene: a prophet like Moses into whose mouth God will put His words. Peter applies it to Jesus, Acts 3:22, and the Father's voice on the mountain of transfiguration says, 'Listen to Him!' Matthew 17:5. Christ exceeds the type because He is not only a messenger standing between; He is the Word made flesh, John 1:14, and the one mediator between God and men, 1 Timothy 2:5. Moses could not bring the people up the mountain; Christ brings His people all the way in, Hebrews 7:25.

typology.type: The tablets written by God's finger (v.22)
typology.fulfillment: God wrote the ten words on stone and gave them to Moses, and they were kept in the ark at the heart of the sanctuary. The stone showed the permanence of the law but also its distance: written outside the people, it could command but not change them. Paul draws the contrast directly, calling believers a letter written 'not on tablets of stone but on tablets of human hearts' by the Spirit of the living God, 2 Corinthians 3:3. The promise of Jeremiah 31:33, restated in Hebrews 8:10, is the same law written within. The type falls short because stone tablets could be broken, and were; the Spirit's writing endures.

typology.type: The Sabbath rest given to the slave and the stranger (vv.14-15)
typology.fulfillment: Israel's weekly rest remembered release from Egypt and extended it to servants and animals. Jesus announced His ministry as liberty for captives and release for the oppressed, Luke 4:18, and chose the Sabbath for acts of release, freeing a woman 'whom Satan has kept bound,' Luke 13:16. He calls Himself Lord of the Sabbath, Mark 2:28. Hebrews 4:9-10 speaks of a Sabbath rest that remains for God's people, entered by resting from one's own works. The weekly day was a shadow, Colossians 2:17; the rest itself is found in Christ, and its final form is the unbroken rest of the new creation.

typology.type: Israel's terror at the fire and the voice (vv.23-26)
typology.fulfillment: The people discovered that a sinful people could hear God and live, verse 24, yet could not bear to go on hearing Him, verse 25. Hebrews 12:18-21 recalls this mountain, the fire, darkness and 'a voice that made its hearers beg that no further word be spoken,' and then says believers have come instead to Mount Zion, to Jesus the mediator of a new covenant, Hebrews 12:22-24. The escalation is startling: the new assembly is joyful, not terrified. Yet Hebrews does not make God less holy; 'our God is a consuming fire,' Hebrews 12:29, quoting Deuteronomy 4:24. The difference is the mediator, not a softer God.

study.christ:
The chapter leads to Christ most directly through its mediator. The people's request in verse 27, 'Go near and listen ... Then you can tell us,' is approved by God, verse 28, and Deuteronomy 18:16-18 draws the line forward: because they asked for a go between at Horeb, God will raise up a prophet like Moses and put His words in his mouth. The New Testament hears Jesus as that prophet. Peter quotes the promise in Acts 3:22 and Stephen in Acts 7:37, and on the mountain of transfiguration, with Moses present, the voice from the cloud says, 'This is My beloved Son ... Listen to Him!' Matthew 17:5. The words echo 'You must listen to him,' Deuteronomy 18:15.

But Christ is more than a greater Moses. John 1:17-18 sets them side by side: the law came through Moses, grace and truth through Jesus Christ, and the Son at the Father's side has made Him known. Moses stood between God and Israel as a man who heard. Jesus stands between as one who is Himself God and Himself man, 1 Timothy 2:5. Galatians 3:19-20 notes that the law was given through a mediator; in Christ the mediator and the God who promises are one.

The chapter also leads to Christ by the law it sets out. Jesus did not abolish these words but fulfilled them, Matthew 5:17. In the Sermon on the Mount He presses the sixth and seventh commands inward, anger as murder and the lustful look as adultery, Matthew 5:21-28, which is the direction the tenth command already pointed. When the rich young man asked about life, Jesus answered with the second table, Matthew 19:18-19, and exposed the one thing the man could not give up. Only one person has kept these commands from the heart. Jesus could say, 'I do exactly what the Father has commanded Me,' John 14:31, and Paul says God sent His Son 'born under the law,' Galatians 4:4, so that 'the righteous standard of the law might be fulfilled in us,' Romans 8:3-4.

Finally, God's longing in verse 29, 'If only they had such a heart,' finds its answer in the new covenant Christ mediates. Hebrews 8:6-10 quotes Jeremiah 31:33, God writing His laws on hearts, and Paul describes believers as letters written by the Spirit on hearts rather than stone, 2 Corinthians 3:3. The Christian reading must stay honest here. The ten words are not a hidden allegory of Jesus. They are God's covenant commands. They lead to Christ because He alone kept them, because He mediates the covenant that writes them within, and because in Him the fear of verse 25 gives way to joyful access, Hebrews 12:22-24.
study.god:
The first thing God says about Himself is His name and His deed: 'I am the LORD your God, who brought you out,' verse 6. The God of the commandments is first the God of the exodus. His authority to command rests on His identity and His grace, and every later command is an outworking of belonging to Him.

He speaks. The chapter stresses the voice more than the sight: 'out of the fire, the cloud, and the deep darkness,' verse 22, in 'a loud voice.' Deuteronomy 4:12 makes the point sharply: 'You heard the sound of the words, but saw no form.' This is why the second command forbids images. God has chosen to make Himself known by word, and no carved shape could represent a God who revealed Himself as voice. The people's confession in verse 26, 'the voice of the living God,' contrasts Him with idols that are made and silent.

He is jealous, verse 9, with the exclusive love of a husband. His jealousy is not insecurity but the proper refusal of a lover to share his beloved with rivals. It carries a warning and a promise that are deliberately unequal. Iniquity is visited to the third and fourth generation 'of those who hate Me,' while loving devotion reaches 'a thousand' generations of those who love Him, verse 10, the BSB footnote noting the Hebrew is literally 'to thousands.' The asymmetry is the point. The generations that suffer are those who continue in hatred, as Ezekiel 18:20 later clarifies; the mercy far outruns the judgment. Exodus 34:6-7 repeats the same pairing in God's revelation of His name.

He is holy. The mountain blazed with fire, and the people concluded that 'this great fire will consume us,' verse 25. They were not wrong about God. Yet the same verses show that He is gracious in the way He meets them. He approves their request, 'They have done well,' verse 28, and provides a mediator rather than demanding that they endure what they cannot bear.

Most tender of all, God reveals desire. 'If only they had such a heart to fear Me and keep all My commandments always, so that it might be well with them and with their children forever,' verse 29. His commands aim at His people's good, and He longs for their obedience because He longs for their welfare. The chapter holds together a God of consuming fire and a God who sighs over His people's hearts. That tension is resolved not by softening His holiness but by His promise to give the heart He asks for, Deuteronomy 30:6.

For worship, the chapter teaches reverence and gratitude together. Believers approach a God who is still a consuming fire, Hebrews 12:28-29, but who has spoken, rescued, and provided the Mediator through whom they draw near.

crossReferences.note: The first account of the ten words and the people's fear. Placed beside Deuteronomy 5, it shows what Moses preserved and what he adjusted for a new generation: 'Remember' becomes 'Observe,' the Sabbath gains the memory of slavery, and the wife moves ahead of the house in the tenth command.

Moses' own commentary on Horeb, delivered just before this chapter. Israel heard a voice but saw no form, and that fact becomes the reason images of God are forbidden. It explains why the second command follows naturally from a God who reveals Himself by speaking.

The people's plea at Horeb, 'Let us not hear the voice of the LORD our God,' is quoted, God's approval, 'They have spoken well,' is repeated, and from it grows the promise of a prophet like Moses. Deuteronomy 5:23-28 is the seedbed of that messianic hope.

Peter, preaching in the temple, identifies Jesus as the prophet like Moses. The line runs from the people's fear in Deuteronomy 5, through the promise of Deuteronomy 18, to the risen Christ, whom all must now hear and obey.

Recalls the mountain of this chapter, fire, darkness and a voice the hearers begged to stop, and sets against it Mount Zion and Jesus the mediator of a new covenant. The contrast is not between a harsh God and a gentle one, since verse 29 still calls Him a consuming fire, but between two ways of approach.

God's wish in Deuteronomy 5:29 for a people with 'such a heart' becomes a promise: a new covenant in which the law is written on the heart rather than on stone. Hebrews 8:10 quotes it as the covenant Jesus mediates.

Paul takes up the tablets of stone from Deuteronomy 5:22 and contrasts them with the Spirit's writing on 'tablets of human hearts.' The same law, once external, is now inscribed within by the living God.

Jesus takes the sixth and seventh words and presses them to the heart, anger and the lustful look. He is not adding to the law but drawing out the inward direction already present in the tenth command, which forbids desire itself.

Paul says the tenth command, 'Do not covet,' is what made him aware of sin. Because it forbids a desire rather than an act, it exposes the heart that the other commands might leave hidden, and so shows why a new heart is needed.

Paul lists the neighbour commands of Deuteronomy 5:17-21 and sums them up in 'Love your neighbor as yourself,' Leviticus 19:18. The second table is not replaced by love; it describes what love refuses to do to a neighbour.

Paul quotes Deuteronomy 5:16 with its promise, 'that it may go well with you,' a phrase Deuteronomy adds to the Exodus wording. He calls it the first commandment with a promise and applies it to children in the church.

Jesus defends healing a crippled woman on the Sabbath as a release from bondage. His argument follows Deuteronomy 5:15, where the Sabbath remembers deliverance from slavery, and shows the day as a sign of liberation rather than a burden.

study.oneStory:
Deuteronomy 5 stands at a hinge in the story. The God who made the world and rested on the seventh day, Genesis 2:2-3, and who rescued Israel from Egypt, now tells His redeemed people who He is and how they are to live with Him. It answers a question raised since Eden: can humanity live in God's presence again? At Horeb the answer is yes and no. God spoke and the people lived, verse 24, but they could not bear to go on hearing Him, verse 25. The garden's closed way, guarded by cherubim, is still closed to a people who come without a mediator.

The chapter also sets up much of what follows. The people's promise, 'we will listen and obey,' verse 27, will be tested and broken, first at the golden calf, then through the judges and the kings, until Israel is sent into exile. The prophets indict them by these very words, Hosea 4:2 and Jeremiah 7:9. God's own sigh in verse 29 shows He knew the problem lay deeper than knowledge. The law was holy, but it was written on stone and the heart was unchanged.

So the story moves toward a new covenant. Deuteronomy 30:6 promises circumcised hearts; Jeremiah 31:33 promises the law written within; Ezekiel 36:26-27 promises a new heart and God's Spirit. Deuteronomy 18 promises a prophet like Moses, and the Gospels present Jesus as that prophet and more, the Son who kept the commands and mediates a better covenant, Hebrews 8:6.

In the new creation the picture of this chapter is transformed. The people who retreated to their tents because the voice was too much will hear the loud voice from the throne announcing that God's dwelling is with humanity, Revelation 21:3. The fear that made Israel beg for distance gives way to the promise that His servants 'will see His face,' Revelation 22:4. The rest the Sabbath pictured will be complete, and the law once written on stone will be simply the way God's people love Him and each other forever.

sermon.title: God's Law
sermon.why: Keller preaches through this restatement of the Ten Commandments, drawing out how the law reveals both the holiness of God and humanity's need for a mediator, pointing forward to the grace that alone can produce heartfelt obedience.

quiz.q: According to verse 3, with whom did the LORD make the covenant at Horeb?

options.text: With this very generation, alive and present, not only with their ancestors.
options.note: Verse 3 states this explicitly, pressing the covenant's claim onto the new generation directly.

options.text: Only with the generation that had already died in the wilderness.
options.note: Verse 3 explicitly denies this, saying the covenant was made with those alive that very day.

options.text: Only with Moses personally.
options.note: The text says the covenant was made with the whole assembly, not Moses alone.

options.text: The verse makes no claim about who the covenant was made with.
options.note: Verse 3 makes a specific and deliberate claim about this.

quiz.q: What reason does Deuteronomy 5:15 give for keeping the Sabbath, distinct from the reason given in Exodus 20:11?

options.text: Remembering that they were slaves in Egypt and that the LORD delivered them with a mighty hand.
options.note: Verse 15 grounds the Sabbath in redemption from slavery, complementing Exodus 20's emphasis on creation.

options.text: Because the seventh day was considered unlucky for travel.
options.note: No such superstition appears; the stated reasoning is theological, tied to the exodus from Egypt.

options.text: Because livestock needed constant labor and could not rest.
options.note: The text specifies rest for livestock as part of the command, the opposite of this option.

options.text: No reason at all is given for the Sabbath in this chapter.
options.note: Verse 15 gives an explicit, stated reason.

quiz.q: How did the people respond to hearing the LORD's voice directly from the fire (vv.24-27)?

options.text: They were afraid they would die and asked Moses to hear from God and relay His words to them instead.
options.note: Verses 25-27 record exactly this fearful request for a mediator.

options.text: They demanded to hear more directly from God, not less.
options.note: The opposite occurred; they wanted less direct exposure to God's voice, not more.

options.text: They ignored the experience entirely.
options.note: Their response is described in vivid, specific detail, not ignored.

options.text: They rejected Moses as their spokesman.
options.note: They specifically asked Moses to be their spokesman, the opposite of rejecting him.

quiz.q: How did the LORD respond to Israel's request for a mediator (vv.28-29)?

options.text: He said they had spoken well, and wished they had a heart to fear Him and keep His commands always.
options.note: Verses 28-29 record God's approving response along with His longing for their lasting faithfulness.

options.text: He rebuked them for their fear as a lack of faith.
options.note: The text records approval of their request, not rebuke.

options.text: He refused to speak to Moses any further.
options.note: The opposite happens; God continues speaking directly to Moses for the people's benefit.

options.text: No response from the LORD is recorded here.
options.note: Verses 28-29 record a clear, specific divine response.

quiz.q: Which commandment addresses an inward desire rather than only an outward act?

options.text: The tenth commandment, against coveting.
options.note: Verse 21 names coveting, an internal desire, as the object of this command.

options.text: The sixth commandment, against murder.
options.note: Murder is an outward act; coveting is the command that specifically targets internal desire.

options.text: The third commandment, about the LORD's name.
options.note: This concerns speech and use of God's name, not an internal desire as such.

options.text: None of the ten commandments address internal desire.
options.note: The tenth commandment explicitly does, naming coveting itself as the sin.

questions: Moses insisted this covenant belonged to the present generation, not just their ancestors. Do you relate to God's commands as truly your own calling today, or as something belonging to a past generation of faith?
Israel's fear of God's direct voice led them to ask for a mediator. How does knowing Christ is now your mediator change the way you approach God, compared to approaching Him on your own?
God said He wished Israel had a heart to keep His commands always, not just in a moment of fear. Where is your obedience currently driven by fear rather than by a heart that loves Him?

The tenth commandment addresses coveting, a desire of the heart before it ever becomes an action. What desire are you nursing right now that has not yet become an outward act, but is already shaping your heart?
The Sabbath command in this chapter is grounded in remembering slavery and deliverance. What rhythms of rest do you need to reclaim as an act of remembering what God has delivered you from?

translationNotes.note: Unlike Exodus 20:11, which grounds the Sabbath in God's rest after creation, this restatement grounds it in Israel's deliverance from slavery in Egypt, adding a redemption motive appropriate for a covenant-renewal generation.
The order of the tenth commandment differs slightly from Exodus 20:17: here the neighbor's wife is named first, before house and field, a variation in emphasis rather than a change in meaning.

'A man can live even if God speaks with him' reflects the ancient assumption that direct exposure to God's holiness was normally fatal, making the people's survival itself a wonder, and their fear understandable.
